newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Duisenberg says prefers monetary targets for ECB.
newsitem.headline: Duisenberg says prefers monetary targets for ECB.

text.p: Dutch central bank president Wim Duisenberg said on Friday he would prefer the European Central Bank (ECB) to pursue a strategy of monetary targeting to achieve price stability.

In a speech prepared for the board meeting of the Banking Federation of the European Union, he also said it would be undesirable if inflationary differences within the European Union were to politicise the interest rate policy of the ECB's Governing Council.
Duisenberg takes over in July as head of the European Monetary Institute (EMI), the forerunner of the ECB.
He was invited to address the federation, which represents commercial banks in the EU.

Duisenberg said monetary targeting and direct inflation targeting were two possible monetary strategies which the ECB could pursue once it is decided in early 1998 which countries would participate in European economic and monetary union (EMU).
But he said the risk of politicisation of ECB monetary policy was higher under direct inflation targeting.
Duisenberg said the differences between the two strategies should not be exaggerated.
"Nevertheless, I profess that the considerations which I have set out lead me so far to have a certain preference for monetary targeting," he said in the speech.
He said monetary targeting, or keeping the expansion of the money supply under control, did not mean that the central bank had to focus exclusively on monetary growth.
"Other aggregates containing information about inflationary prospects, especially in the near future, will be monitored as well," he said.
This strategy also provided for a certain measure of flexibility.
"In this context, I wish to dissociate myself emphatically from those who wont to accuse my colleagues at the Bundesbank of 'rigidity' and 'monetary dogmatism'," he said.

He said the monetary aggregate to be chosen should be sufficiently controllable, there must be a sufficiently stable long-term relationship between the demand for money and its determinants, such as prices, income, interest rates and wealth, and it must have predictive powers as to future inflation.
Turning to the inflation targeting strategy, he said it made use of an intermediate target -- expected inflation -- and used information variables to forecast it.
The variables included changes in wage costs, the exchange rate, commodity prices, equity prices and the money supply.
But Duisenberg said both strategies sought price stability, were forward looking and used an extensive set of indicators.
"As you can see, the two strategies are actually not as different as their names would have us believe," he said.
The different weights assigned to the money supply formed the main distinction between them.
As the two strategies differed so little in daily practice, the EMI had agreed that the ECB would base its choice of strategy on six criteria.
The criteria are effectiveness, accountability, transparency, medium-term orientation, continuity and consistency with the independence of the ECB.
The strategy chosen must not inspire outsiders to meddle in the discussions on interest rate policy.
"It would be undesirable if any inflationary differences within the Union were to lead to politicisation of the interest rate policy within the ECB Governing Council," he said.
"It seems to me that this risk is greater in the case of direct inflation targeting than if monetary targeting were pursued."
